**(B)** diaphragm

The diaphragm is a dome-shaped muscular septum that separates the thoracic and abdominal cavities, and it flattens when it contracts during inspiration. The pleura is the double membrane around each lung, the trachea is the windpipe, and epithelium is a lining tissue, not a partition between cavities.

**(D)** Five

Oxygen must cross the alveolar epithelial cell (into it and out of it, two membranes), then the capillary endothelial cell (in and out, two more), and finally the plasma membrane of the RBC to reach haemoglobin, which makes five. Both the alveolar wall and the capillary wall are single layers of squamous epithelium, which is why the path is so short even though it crosses five membranes.

[Note: the chapter describes the respiratory membrane but does not count the membranes; standard biology gives five.]

**(A)** Larynx

The larynx, or voice box, contains the elastic true vocal cords, and voice is produced as air passes between them. The pharynx is a common passage for food and air, tonsils are lymphoid organs, and the trachea only conducts air to the lungs.

**(B)** I.R.V.

Inspiratory reserve volume is the maximum extra volume of air that can be inspired by forced breathing in addition to the tidal volume, about 2000 to 3000 ml. Residual volume is what stays in the lungs after maximum expiration, and vital capacity is the sum of tidal volume, IRV and ERV, so it is not an amount "in addition to T.V."

**(D)** Diaphragm

During inspiration the external intercostal muscles contract to raise the ribs and sternum, and at the same time the diaphragm contracts, flattens and moves down. Together they enlarge the thorax, lower the pressure in the lungs and draw air in. Abdominal, jaw and bronchial muscles are not the partners of the external intercostals in normal breathing.

**(B)** cyclosis

Cyclosis is the streaming movement of cytoplasm, seen in *Amoeba*, *Paramoecium* and root hair cells, and it carries materials within the cell. Diffusion is movement of molecules down a concentration gradient, circulation is movement of body fluids through vessels or cavities, and thrombosis is clot formation inside a vessel.

**(C)** Butterfly

A butterfly is an arthropod, and arthropods have an open circulation in which blood flows through body cavities (haemocoels). Earthworm (an annelid), rabbit and shark (vertebrates) all have closed circulation, in which blood stays inside vessels.

**(D)** leucocytes

Leucocytes are amoeboid cells that squeeze out through the pores in capillary walls; this movement is called diapedesis. Erythrocytes and thrombocytes are carried passively in the blood and do not do this, and adipocytes are fat cells of connective tissue, not blood cells.

**(A)** SA node

The sino-atrial node in the right atrium generates each new wave of contraction and sets its pace, so it is the pacemaker. The AV node is called the pace setter, and the bundle of His and Purkinje fibres only conduct the impulse through the ventricles.

**(A)** Red blood corpuscle

Mature human erythrocytes are enucleated and also lack mitochondria, leaving more room for haemoglobin. Neutrophils, basophils and lymphocytes are white blood cells, and all leucocytes are nucleated.

**(A)** Open

Cockroach is an arthropod, and its blood flows through body cavities (haemocoels) rather than in a closed network of vessels, so its circulation is open. Closed and double circulation belong to vertebrates such as birds and mammals, and "lymphatic" is a part of the circulatory system, not a type of it.

**(B)** WBC

White blood cells escape through the fenestrae in capillary walls by amoeboid movement, a process called diapedesis, to reach sites of infection. RBCs and platelets stay in the bloodstream, and neurons are not blood cells at all.

**(C)** Eustachian valve

The opening of the inferior vena cava (postcaval) into the right atrium is guarded by the Eustachian valve. The Thebesian valve guards the opening of the coronary sinus, and the tricuspid and bicuspid valves guard the right and left atrioventricular apertures.

**(A)** P

The P-wave, a small upward deflection, represents atrial depolarization. The QRS complex represents ventricular depolarization and the T-wave ventricular repolarization, while Q is only the first downward part of the QRS complex.

**(C)** interstitial fluid

The fluid that bathes tissue cells in the intercellular spaces is interstitial fluid (tissue fluid), as the lymphatic system figure labels it. Once this fluid enters the lymphatic vessels it is called lymph, so lymph is the fluid inside lymphatics rather than in the spaces between cells; blood stays inside blood vessels, and water is only one component of these fluids.
